tabs.casual: V았/었어요 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V았/었어요 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Take the verb stem. If the last vowel of the stem is ㅏ or ㅗ, add 았어요; all other vowels add 었어요. Contracted stems: 하다 → 했어요; 오다 → 왔어요; 보다 → 봤어요. Irregular ㅂ stems drop ㅂ and add 웠어요 (춥다 → 추웠어요). Irregular ㄷ stems change ㄷ to ㄹ before 었어요 (듣다 → 들었어요). Irregular ㅅ stems drop ㅅ (낫다 → 나았어요). Irregular 르 stems: 모르다 → 몰랐어요, 다르다 → 달랐어요. Contrast with V-고 있었어요 (past progressive) and V았/었었어요 (remote past / past-perfect nuance). The doubled past 았/었었어요 signals an action that was true in the past but is no longer true: 살았었어요 = 'I used to live there (but no longer do)'. Avoid confusing the ㅂ-irregular past 웠어요 with the future -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
usage: I went to Korea last year.
I learned piano when I was young.
examples: I went to Korea last year.
I learned piano when I was young.

tabs.casual: V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Take the verb stem. After a vowel-final stem add -ㄹ 거예요 (가다 → 갈 거예요, 하다 → 할 거예요). After a consonant-final stem add -을 거예요 (먹다 → 먹을 거예요, 읽다 → 읽을 거예요). ㄹ-final stems attach -ㄹ 거예요 directly (살다 → 살 거예요). For first-person use with intention; for third-person it expresses inference about the future. Contrast with V-(으)ㄹ게요 (first-person promise/commitment only) and A/V-겠- (volition or inference based on sensory evidence). V-(으)ㄹ 거예요 is the general-purpose future and is also used for inference (third person).
usage: I will meet a friend tomorrow.
I am going to finish reading this book.
그 사람은 지금 자고 있을 거예요.
That person is probably sleeping right now.
examples: I will meet a friend tomorrow.
I am going to finish reading this book.

tabs.casual: V기 전에 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V기 전에 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach 기 전에 directly to the plain (dictionary) verb stem regardless of vowel/consonant ending.
usage: I brush my teeth before sleeping.
I checked the map before departing.
Submit the homework before class starts.
examples: I brush my teeth before sleeping.
I checked the map before departing.

tabs.casual: V-습니다 / ㅂ니다 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V-습니다 / ㅂ니다 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Declarative: consonant-final stem + 습니다 (먹다 → 먹습니다); vowel-final or ㄹ-final stem + ㅂ니다 (가다 → 갑니다, 살다 → 삽니다 — ㄹ drops).
usage: This product is of excellent quality.

tabs.casual: -(으)시- (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: -(으)시- with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Insert -(으)시- between the verb stem and the tense/mood ending to honor the subject.
usage: Where do you live? to a respected person
The director is not in right now.
examples: Where do you live? to a respected person

tabs.casual: V이/히/리/기다 (passive) (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V이/히/리/기다 (passive) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Four suffixes attach to specific verb stems to create passive verbs: -이- (보다 → 보이다, 쓰다 → 쓰이다), -히- (읽다 → 읽히다, 잡다 → 잡히다), -리- (팔다 → 팔리다, 듣다 → 들리다), -기- (안다 → 안기다, 막다 → 막히다).
usage: Music can be heard from far away.
That book is read a lot.
The baby was held by the mother.
examples: Music can be heard from far away.
That book is read a lot.

tabs.casual: V이/히/리/기/우/추/구다 (causative) (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V이/히/리/기/우/추/구다 (causative) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Seven suffixes make a verb mean 'cause someone to do/be X': -이- (먹다 → 먹이다 'feed'), -히- (앉다 → 앉히다 'seat'), -리- (울다 → 울리다 'make cry'), -기- (신다 → 신기다 'put shoes on'), -우- (자다 → 재우다 'put to sleep', 서다 → 세우다), -추- (낮다 → 낮추다 'lower'), -구- (rare).
usage: I put the baby to sleep.
examples: I put the baby to sleep.

tabs.casual: N에게 / 한테 / 께 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: N에게 / 한테 / 께 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach directly to a noun. 에게 is written/formal; 한테 is colloquial; 께 is honorific. Direction 'to': 친구에게 편지를 써요. Direction 'from': add 서 to the dative — 에게서 / 한테서 / 께서. For non-person recipients use N에 not N에게. Distinguish N에게서 (from a person) from N에서 (from a place). The particle 한테 is identical in function to 에게 but is conversational — do not use in formal writing.
usage: I sent a text to a friend.
I will ask the teacher. honorific
I gave food to the dog.
My parents gave me pocket money.
examples: I sent a text to a friend.
I will ask the teacher. honorific
I gave food to the dog.

tabs.casual: N와/과 / 하고 / (이)랑 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: N와/과 / 하고 / (이)랑 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: 와 attaches after a vowel-final noun; 과 after a consonant-final noun.
usage: I bought apples and pears. written
I watched a movie with a friend. spoken
I went with my older brother and older sister.
I ate rice and soup. formal/written
examples: I bought apples and pears. written
I watched a movie with a friend. spoken
I went with my older brother and older sister.

tabs.casual: N밖에 + 부정 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: N밖에 + 부정 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach 밖에 directly to a noun. The predicate MUST be negative: 없다, 안 V, 못 V, V지 않다. N밖에 없어요 = 'there is only N / nothing but N'. Using 밖에 with a positive predicate is ungrammatical. Contrast with N만 (only N, takes a positive predicate). N밖에 emphasizes scarcity or restriction — the speaker feels the amount is insufficient. 밖에 없다 is very common and should be memorized as a chunk.

tabs.casual: N이나 (approximation / 'about N') (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: N이나 (approximation / 'about N') with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach 이나 after a consonant-final noun/numeral, 나 after a vowel-final noun/numeral.
usage: I waited for three whole hours.
I drank as many as five cups of coffee.
The distance is as far as 10 kilometers.
examples: I waited for three whole hours.
I drank as many as five cups of coffee.

tabs.casual: N이라도 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: N이라도 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach 이라도 after a consonant-final noun, 라도 after a vowel-final noun.
usage: At least have a cup of tea.
I want to meet you even if just for a moment.
Should I at least bring you some water?
오늘 안 되면 내일이라도 와 주세요.
If today doesn't work, please come at least tomorrow.
examples: At least have a cup of tea.
I want to meet you even if just for a moment.
Should I at least bring you some water?

tabs.casual: -네요 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: -네요 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach 네요 to a verb/adjective stem as a sentence-final ending.
usage: Oh, this is really delicious! — just tasted it
Oh, the weather is nice today. noticing
Oh, you speak Korean well! impressed realization
examples: Oh, this is really delicious! — just tasted it
Oh, the weather is nice today. noticing

tabs.casual: -군요 / -구나 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: -군요 / -구나 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Polite form: verb/adjective stem + 군요. For action verbs in present tense add 는 before 군요: V-는군요. For descriptive verbs attach directly: A-군요. Casual/intimate form: -구나. Past: V/A-았/었군요. Expresses the speaker's sudden realization or surprise — often a monologue-type exclamation. Contrast with -네요 (pattern-113): -네요 is more common in everyday speech and implies direct sensory discovery; -군요 is slightly more literary/formal. -구나 is used in casual speech or when talking to oneself / to a child. 그렇군요 is a very common filler meaning 'I see / is that so?'.
usage: Oh, I see. I didn't know that.
Oh, you're a student! — casual, to oneself
Oh, that must have been really hard for you.
examples: Oh, I see. I didn't know that.
Oh, you're a student! — casual, to oneself

tabs.casual: -(으)ㄹ걸요 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: -(으)ㄹ걸요 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach -(으)ㄹ걸요 as a sentence-final ending.
usage: I think they've probably arrived by now.
I should have left earlier. regret, casual
I think it will rain tomorrow.
examples: I think they've probably arrived by now.
I should have left earlier. regret, casual

tabs.casual: V았/었으면 좋겠어요 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V았/었으면 좋겠어요 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Form: V-았으면 좋겠어요 (after ㅏ/ㅗ vowel stem) or V-었으면 좋겠어요 (after other vowels); 하다 → 했으면 좋겠어요.
usage: I wish the weather were nice.
I hope you get better soon.
I wish I could win the lottery.
I wish I could go together with you.
examples: I wish the weather were nice.
I hope you get better soon.
I wish I could win the lottery.

tabs.casual: V-는지 / (으)ㄴ지 / (으)ㄹ지 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V-는지 / (으)ㄴ지 / (으)ㄹ지 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Embedded question endings transforming a question into a subordinate clause.
usage: I don't know what to eat.
Do you know where that person is?
Check whether the weather is good.
I am curious when they will arrive.
examples: I don't know what to eat.
Do you know where that person is?
Check whether the weather is good.

tabs.casual: N의 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: N의 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach 의 to a noun to mark possession or modification: N의 N = 'N's N'.
usage: The capital of Korea is Seoul.
In my opinion, it seems right.
examples: The capital of Korea is Seoul.
In my opinion, it seems right.

hangul: 수 분 개 명 권 ... (단위 명사)
romanization: su bun gae myeong gwon ... (danwi myeongsa)

tabs.casual: 수 분 개 명 권 ... (단위 명사) (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.polite: 수 분 개 명 권 ... (단위 명사) (polite/default study form)
tabs.formal: 수 분 개 명 권 ... (단위 명사) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Korean quantities use native or Sino-Korean numbers plus a counter.
usage: I drank two cups of coffee.
examples: I drank two cups of coffee.

tabs.casual: ㅂ 불규칙 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: ㅂ 불규칙 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Verbs/adjectives whose stem ends in ㅂ: when the next syllable begins with a vowel, ㅂ changes to 우 (돕다 → 도와, 곱다 → 고와 are exceptions using 오).
usage: The weather is cold. 춥다 + 어요
This food is spicy. 맵다 + 어요
It is easy today. 쉽다 + 어요
examples: The weather is cold. 춥다 + 어요
This food is spicy. 맵다 + 어요

tabs.casual: ㄷ 불규칙 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: ㄷ 불규칙 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Verbs whose stem ends in ㄷ: when the next syllable begins with a vowel, ㄷ changes to ㄹ.
usage: I listen to music. 듣다 irregular
I walked in the park. 걷다 irregular
I close the door. 닫다 regular
I will ask the teacher. 묻다 irregular
examples: I listen to music. 듣다 irregular
I walked in the park. 걷다 irregular
I close the door. 닫다 regular

tabs.casual: ㅅ 불규칙 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: ㅅ 불규칙 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Verbs/adjectives whose stem ends in ㅅ: when the next syllable begins with a vowel, ㅅ drops entirely.
usage: I hope you get better quickly. 낫다 irregular
They built a house. 짓다 irregular
examples: I hope you get better quickly. 낫다 irregular
They built a house. 짓다 irregular

tabs.casual: 르 불규칙 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: 르 불규칙 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Verbs/adjectives whose stem ends in 르: when the next syllable is 아요 or 어요, ㄹ is doubled onto the preceding syllable and 으 is dropped: 모르다 → 몰라요, 다르다 → 달라요, 빠르다 → 빨라요, 부르다 → 불러요, 고르다 → 골라요, 자르다 → 잘라요.
usage: I don't know that name. 모르다 → 몰라요
The two people are different. 다르다 → 달라요
I sang a song. 부르다 → 불렀어요
examples: I don't know that name. 모르다 → 몰라요
The two people are different. 다르다 → 달라요
I sang a song. 부르다 → 불렀어요

tabs.casual: ㅎ 불규칙 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: ㅎ 불규칙 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Adjectives whose stem ends in ㅎ: before -아/어요, ㅎ drops and ending becomes 애요: 빨갛다 → 빨개요, 파랗다 → 파래요, 노랗다 → 노래요, 하얗다 → 하얘요, 그렇다 → 그래요, 이렇다 → 이래요, 저렇다 → 저래요, 어떻다 → 어때요.
usage: The sky is blue. 파랗다 → 파래요
The rose is red. 빨갛다 → 빨개요
How is that person? 어떻다 → 어때요
White snow is falling. 하얗다 → 하얀 + 눈
examples: The sky is blue. 파랗다 → 파래요
The rose is red. 빨갛다 → 빨개요
How is that person? 어떻다 → 어때요

tabs.casual: A/V-겠- (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: A/V-겠- with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Insert 겠 between the verb stem and the sentence-final ending.
usage: I will do my best. formal commitment
That looks delicious! inference from sight
Yes, I understand. fixed polite expression
It must be really cold there.
examples: I will do my best. formal commitment
That looks delicious! inference from sight
Yes, I understand. fixed polite expression

tabs.casual: V-(으)ㄴ/는데 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V-(으)ㄴ/는데 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attaches to a verb or adjective stem as a connective ending providing background context, scene-setting, or mild contrast for the main clause.
usage: I'm hungry — what should we eat?
This movie is interesting, but it's a bit long.
I met a friend yesterday — it was so nice to see them.
Actually, I don't know either, you see.
examples: I'm hungry — what should we eat?
This movie is interesting, but it's a bit long.
I met a friend yesterday — it was so nice to see them.

tabs.casual: 따라서 / 그러나 / 반면에 / 즉 / 결국 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.polite: 따라서 / 그러나 / 반면에 / 즉 / 결국 (polite/default study form)
tabs.formal: 따라서 / 그러나 / 반면에 / 즉 / 결국 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Sentence-initial discourse connectors for formal writing, essays, and academic discourse.
usage: 연습이 중요하다. 따라서 매일 해야 한다.
Practice is important. Therefore, you must do it every day.
그는 열심히 했다. 그러나 결과가 좋지 않았다.
He worked hard. However, the result was not good.
두 방법은 다르다. 반면에 목표는 같다.
The two methods are different. On the other hand, the goal is the same.
This is, namely, the key point.
examples: 연습이 중요하다. 따라서 매일 해야 한다.

그는 열심히 했다. 그러나 결과가 좋지 않았다.

두 방법은 다르다. 반면에 목표는 같다.

tabs.casual: V/A-아/어지다 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V/A-아/어지다 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach -아/어지다 to a verb/adjective stem following vowel harmony (ㅏ/ㅗ → 아지다; other vowels → 어지다; 하다 → 해지다).
usage: This product was made in Korea.
My heart/mind has become at ease.
examples: This product was made in Korea.

tabs.casual: V-아/어 놓다 / 두다 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V-아/어 놓다 / 두다 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach -아/어 놓다 or -아/어 두다 following vowel harmony.
usage: 내일을 위해 밥을 미리 만들어 놨어요.
I made rice in advance for tomorrow.
Write down the important content and keep it.
You can leave the luggage here.
examples: 내일을 위해 밥을 미리 만들어 놨어요.
I made rice in advance for tomorrow.
Write down the important content and keep it.

tabs.casual: V/A-다면 / N이라면 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V/A-다면 / N이라면 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attaches as a connective ending expressing a hypothetical or counterfactual condition — stronger than plain -(으)면.
usage: If I were a bird, I would fly away.
If you had lots of money, what would you do?
If you had spoken up then, things would have changed.
If you are a student, there is a discount.
examples: If I were a bird, I would fly away.

tabs.casual: V-고 있다 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V-고 있다 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach -고 있다 to the plain verb stem regardless of ending.

tabs.casual: A/V-아/어 보이다 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: A/V-아/어 보이다 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach -아/어 보이다 to a descriptive verb (adjective) stem following vowel harmony.
usage: The weather looks nice — shall we go out?

tabs.casual: ㅂ-변칙 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: ㅂ-변칙 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: When a stem ends in ㅂ (e.g. 덥-), replace ㅂ with 우 before any vowel-initial ending: 덥 + 어요 → 더 + 우 + 어요 → 더워요.

tabs.casual: ㄷ-변칙 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: ㄷ-변칙 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: When a stem ends in ㄷ (e.g. 듣-), change ㄷ → ㄹ before any vowel-initial ending: 듣 + 어요 → 들어요.

tabs.casual: ㅅ-변칙 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: ㅅ-변칙 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: When a stem ends in ㅅ (e.g. 짓-), drop ㅅ before any vowel-initial ending: 짓 + 어요 → 지어요.

tabs.casual: ㄹ-탈락 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: ㄹ-탈락 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Stems ending in ㄹ (e.g. 알-) drop ㄹ before -(으)ㄴ, -(으)ㄹ, -ㅂ니다, -세요, -ㄴ다: 알 + ㄴ → 아는, 알 + ㅂ니다 → 압니다, 알 + 세요 → 아세요.

tabs.casual: ㅎ-변칙 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: ㅎ-변칙 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Adjective stems ending in ㅎ (e.g. 빨갛-) drop ㅎ and the stem vowel ㅏ/ㅓ contracts with the ending vowel ㅏ/ㅓ → ㅐ: 빨갛 + 아요 → 빨가 + 아요 → 빨개요.
usage: Please give me a red apple.
examples: Please give me a red apple.

tabs.casual: 르-변칙 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: 르-변칙 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Stems ending in 르 (e.g. 모르-) replace 르 with ㄹㄹ and drop 으 before 아/어 endings: 모르 + 아요 → 몰 + 라요 → 몰라요.

tabs.casual: N도 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: N도 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach 도 directly to a noun, replacing 은/는/이/가/을/를.

tabs.casual: N만 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: N만 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach 만 directly to the noun. It replaces 은/는/이/가/을/를 but follows place/time particles: 여기서만 'only here'. Contrast with 밖에: 만 can appear in positive sentences, 밖에 cannot. 만 is neutral — it does not express surprise or judgment about the quantity. Compare: 물만 마셔요 (I drink only water, neutral) vs. 물밖에 못 마셔요 (I can drink nothing but water, implies restriction/hardship).

tabs.formal: N이었어요 / 였어요 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: N이었어요 after consonant-final nouns; N였어요 after vowel-final nouns.

tabs.casual: N인데 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: N인데 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: N이다 + -(으)ㄴ데 = 인데 (always 인데 regardless of final consonant).
usage: I'm a student, and I have a question.

It's the weekend — what are you doing?

tabs.casual: N이라서 / 라서 (casual form depends on the final ending)

tabs.casual: V-았/었으면 좋겠어요 (counterfactual wish) (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V-았/었으면 좋겠어요 (counterfactual wish) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Past tense marker + -으면. With 좋겠어요: expresses a wish that something were different now (simple counterfactual wish). Despite the past morpheme, refers to present or future unmet conditions. Stronger than present 으면 좋겠어요, which can express open future hopes. Contrast with V-았/었더라면 (pattern-153, stronger counterfactual with stated regret and result clause). 았/었으면 좋겠어요 is a complete sentence by itself; 았/었더라면 typically pairs with -았/었을 텐데 or -았/었을 거예요.
usage: I wish I had known a bit earlier.
I wish we could go together.
I wish I had said it then.
I wish I had more money.
examples: I wish I had known a bit earlier.
I wish we could go together.
I wish I had said it then.

tabs.casual: V-았/었더라면 … -았/었을 텐데 (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V-았/었더라면 … -았/었을 텐데 with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Past marker + -더라면: strongly counterfactual, implies the condition was definitively not met.
usage: 그때 포기하지 않았더라면 지금쯤 성공했을 텐데.
If I hadn't given up then, I would probably be successful by now.
If you hadn't helped me, I would have failed.
If you had come early, you would have seen it.
If I had said that, things would have changed.
examples: 그때 포기하지 않았더라면 지금쯤 성공했을 텐데.
If I hadn't given up then, I would probably be successful by now.
If you hadn't helped me, I would have failed.
If you had come early, you would have seen it.

tabs.casual: A/V-네요 (fresh realisation, sentence-final) (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: A/V-네요 (fresh realisation, sentence-final) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Attach 네요 directly to the predicate stem as a sentence-final ending.
usage: Korean is more interesting than I thought — I'm just realising this.
Oh, you've come! — noticing someone's arrival
So that's how it turned out.
It's not as hard as I thought.
examples: Korean is more interesting than I thought — I'm just realising this.
Oh, you've come! — noticing someone's arrival

tabs.formal: A/V-군요 / V-는군요 (exclamatory polite) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Stronger surprise or exclamation than 네요; often used when the speaker is more visibly impressed or realising something significant.
usage: It's already been 10 years! — surprised exclamation
Oh, it has changed a lot!
Oh, so that's how it happened.
examples: It's already been 10 years! — surprised exclamation
Oh, it has changed a lot!

tabs.casual: V-(으)ㄹ걸요 (regret / hedged assertion) (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V-(으)ㄹ걸요 (regret / hedged assertion) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Dual function: (1) retrospective regret (1st person) — I should have done X; (2) confident hedged assertion — I bet X is the case.
usage: I should have said something then. mild regret
They've probably figured it out by now. assertion
I bet that person has already left.
examples: I should have said something then. mild regret
They've probably figured it out by now. assertion

tabs.casual: V-았/었을 텐데 (unfulfilled expectation) (casual form depends on the final ending)
tabs.formal: V-았/었을 텐데 (unfulfilled expectation) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Past + -(으)ㄹ 텐데: expresses the speaker's expectation or assumption that a past condition would have held, implying it did not or may not have.
usage: If you'd come early, you would have seen it.
If you had said it then, things would have been different.
If you had practiced more, you would have done well.
If I had known, I would have helped.
examples: If you'd come early, you would have seen it.
If you had said it then, things would have been different.
If you had practiced more, you would have done well.

tabs.casual: N이/가 vs N은/는 (discourse contrast) (casual form depends on the final ending)

tabs.formal: N이/가 vs N은/는 (discourse contrast) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Use 이/가 when the noun phrase is new to the discourse, answers an implicit 'who/what' question, or exhaustively identifies the subject ('It is specifically N and not others').
usage: A friend called yesterday. — new info: the call-maker is the friend
This one is expensive, but that one is cheap. — contrast with 은/는
As for elephants, their noses are long. — topic + subject
Who did it? I did. — 이/가 for exhaustive identification
examples: A friend called yesterday. — new info: the call-maker is the friend
This one is expensive, but that one is cheap. — contrast with 은/는
As for elephants, their noses are long. — topic + subject

tabs.formal: 따라서 / 그러므로 (formal conclusion connectors) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: Sentence-initial discourse connectors signalling logical conclusion in formal writing.
usage: 실험 결과가 가설을 뒷받침했다. 따라서 이 이론은 유효하다고 볼 수 있다.
The experiment results supported the hypothesis. Therefore, this theory can be considered valid.
비용이 너무 많다. 그러므로 이 계획은 수정이 필요하다.
The cost is too high. Therefore, this plan needs revision.
증거가 충분하다. 따라서 결론을 내릴 수 있다.
The evidence is sufficient. Therefore, we can draw a conclusion.
수요가 줄었다. 그러므로 생산을 줄여야 한다.
Demand has decreased. Therefore, production must be reduced.
examples: 실험 결과가 가설을 뒷받침했다. 따라서 이 이론은 유효하다고 볼 수 있다.

formNote: 그러나 = formal written direct contrast/reversal (formal equivalent of 하지만).
usage: 그는 열심히 했다. 그러나 결과가 좋지 않았다.
He worked hard. However, the result was not good.
A국의 경제는 성장했다. 반면에 B국은 침체를 겪었다.
Country A's economy grew. In contrast, Country B experienced stagnation.
정부는 새 정책을 발표했다. 한편, 시민 단체들은 반발했다.
The government announced a new policy. Meanwhile, civic groups pushed back.
이 방법은 빠르다. 반면에 저 방법은 정확하다.
This method is fast. On the other hand, that method is accurate.
examples: 그는 열심히 했다. 그러나 결과가 좋지 않았다.
He worked hard. However, the result was not good.
A국의 경제는 성장했다. 반면에 B국은 침체를 겪었다.
Country A's economy grew. In contrast, Country B experienced stagnation.

tabs.formal: 즉 / 다시 말해서 (written clarification) with formal endings or written-register equivalents when needed

formNote: 즉 ('that is, namely') introduces a restatement or specification of the previous clause.
usage: 이 계획은 비용이 너무 많이 든다. 즉, 현실적이지 않다는 뜻이다.
This plan costs too much. That is, it is not realistic.
그는 매일 운동한다. 다시 말해서, 건강 관리를 매우 중시한다.
He exercises every day. In other words, he values health management greatly.
세 가지 조건이 모두 필요하다. 즉, 어느 하나라도 빠지면 안 된다.
All three conditions are necessary. Namely, none can be missing.
이것이 핵심이다. 다시 말해서, 가장 중요한 부분이다.
This is the key point. In other words, it is the most important part.
examples: 이 계획은 비용이 너무 많이 든다. 즉, 현실적이지 않다는 뜻이다.
This plan costs too much. That is, it is not realistic.

formNote: After certain final consonants, a following plain stop ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, or ㅅ is pronounced tense.
usage: 국밥 is pronounced with tense ㅃ.
먹고 has tense ㄲ after the final ㄱ.
닫다 has tense ㄸ in the second syllable.
examples: 국밥 is pronounced with tense ㅃ.
